newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Krupp sees no problems solved in EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Krupp sees no problems solved in EMU delay.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Monday worries were unfounded that the new single European currency would be unstable if public budget deficits were not exactly at 3.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to qualify for the euro.

Krupp also said the best outcome for the start of the new currency, slated for January 1999, is for the most nations as possible to qualify but for entry criteria in the Maastricht Treaty not to be weakened.
"Worries about the stability of the Euro because an on-target landing on 3.0 percent (deficit of GDP) was not achieved are not warranted," Krupp said.
"We have achieved great stability in Europe but that is often overlooked," he said.

Krupp, saying a delay in the euro's start was no solution to the problem of European nations seeking to meet the Maastricht Treaty critera, also said Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer has made clear the treaty does not say "3.0 percent" in reference to public budget deficits.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has repeatedly said the Maastricht Treaty should be interpreted as saying the budget deficit must be at 3.0 percent in 1997, the year when nations are judged on whether they can join the new currency.
Krupp said: "Tietmeyer has not said what does not conform to the treaty. Therefore he has not said 3.0 (percent)."
